603.title: The pure spring
603.hook: curse a clear spring and it keeps flowing clear (Meditations 8.51)
603.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use the spring as a picture after an insult: they let the sting register, then turn their attention back to what they meant to do anyway, and let the words settle and wash out.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was George Long, whose translation says don't think of the whole of your life at once. Your line was this piece only.

A spring in the hills, the water so clear you can count the pebbles. Someone stands at the edge and shouts at it. Calls it names. Kicks dirt into it. What does the spring do? Nothing dramatic. It keeps coming up from below, and in a minute the water's clear again. Marcus put that picture in book eight, right after imagining the worst that people could do to him.

segments.voice: The entry starts bluntly: suppose people kill you, cut you to pieces, curse you. What can any of that do to stop your mind from staying pure, wise, sober and just? He isn't saying it wouldn't hurt. He's asking what it can reach. Then the spring. Imagine, he says, someone standing beside a clear, sweet spring and cursing it. The spring doesn't stop sending up good water. Throw in mud, or worse, and it quickly scatters it, washes it out, and isn't stained. It isn't defending itself; it's still flowing from below, faster than the dirt can settle. So how, Marcus asks, can you have an ever-flowing spring inside you, and not just a well, a still pit that holds whatever is thrown in? His answer: keep shaping yourself, hour by hour, toward freedom, with kindness, simplicity and modesty. A well depends on what reaches it. A spring has its own source. This isn't pretending an insult didn't land. Even a clear spring goes cloudy for a moment. The point is what happens next: whether the mud sinks in and stays, or gets carried off by what keeps rising. Earlier in the same entry Marcus gives himself a short list: don't be sluggish in action, or muddled in conversation, or wandering in thought. The spring is that list, kept running.

604.title: Light poured out
604.hook: sunlight seems poured down but is never used up (Meditations 8.57)
604.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus use sunlight as a daily reminder: a few minutes in the light, and then attention given to others the way it falls, steady and unforced.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was fountain, the spring that keeps rising. Your line was the spring runs clear.

Sit in a room with one window on a sunny afternoon and watch the patch of light on the floor. It's been pouring in all day, more every minute, and the window never runs dry. The sun never sends a bill. Nobody has to refill it. In book eight of his Meditations, Marcus noticed the same plain thing, sunlight coming in, and found in it a picture of how a mind should move through the world.

segments.voice: The sun's light seems poured down, Marcus says, spread out in every direction, and yet it isn't poured away. It isn't used up. The spreading is a kind of stretching out. Then a word game. The Greek word for rays is aktines, and Marcus says they're called that from a verb meaning to be stretched out. It's his own word play; the point isn't the dictionary but the picture: light reaches out without leaving its source. Next, watch sunlight come through a narrow opening into a dark house. It travels in a straight line, and when it meets something solid that blocks it, it rests there. It doesn't slide off or fall. It just lights up what's in front of it. That's how Marcus wants his own mind to pour itself out: not emptied, not crashing violently into whatever stands in the way, but resting on it, lighting whatever will take the light. And if something refuses it, he says, that thing only deprives itself. So attention, warmth, effort, given like sunlight, can reach far and still not run out, as long as they're poured, not thrown.

605.title: Teach or bear with them
605.hook: people exist for one another: teach them, or bear with them (Meditations 8.59)
605.howItsDone: People who live by this line of Marcus often make the choice consciously when someone frustrates them: either explain once, kindly, or let it go without resentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was aktines, rays that pour out without being used up. Your line was poured out.

Somebody at work does it wrong again. Same report, same mistake, same cheerful shrug. You have a few options. Explain it, one more time. Let it go. Or the third thing, the one that tends to happen without anyone deciding on it: stew, complain about them to someone else, and slowly come to dislike them. Marcus has an entry in book eight only two short sentences long, and it leaves that third option out.
screen: `THE SAME MISTAKE AGAIN.` → `THREE OPTIONS.` → `TEACH OR BEAR WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them.” That's the whole entry. The reason comes first: people are for each other. The idea comes back again and again in the Meditations. We're made to work together, like hands, or feet, or eyelids, or the rows of upper and lower teeth, an image he used back in book two. If that's true, the person who frustrates you is still someone you exist for. Then two doors. If you can show them a better way, teach. Not lecture, not win: teach, which means you actually want them to understand. And if you can't, because they won't listen, or it isn't your place, or you've already tried, then bear with them. Put up with them. Carry it. Now notice what isn't on the list: resent them, gossip about them, write them off. Marcus doesn't argue against those here. He just doesn't offer them, and so the note quietly shuts that third door. It works in both directions, too. Somewhere, someone is deciding right now whether to teach you or bear with you.

606.title: For one another
606.hook: nature made us for one another, so wronging others wrongs the whole (Meditations 9.1)
606.tomorrow: Death as a work of nature
606.howItsDone: Readers who take this passage to heart often treat small wrongs as worth fixing even when no one would notice: returning the extra change, correcting the excuse, giving the credit back.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was third door, the one Marcus leaves out when he says teach or bear. Your line was teach or bear.

A cashier gives you too much change. Ten dollars, maybe. Nobody saw. The store is big; it'll never notice. There may be a small tug anyway, even if it's hard to say why. Book nine of the Meditations opens with Marcus's answer, and it's bigger than ten dollars. A wrong like that, he says, isn't only against the cashier. It's against the whole.

Marcus opens book nine with a startling sentence: whoever acts unjustly acts impiously. A wrong done to a person is also a wrong against the order of things itself. His reason: nature made rational beings for one another, to help each other as each deserves, and never to harm. So harming someone isn't just breaking a rule. It's working against what you were made for, and against the nature of the whole, which Marcus here calls the most ancient of divinities. He doesn't stop at cheating. Lying is impiety too, because the nature of the whole is truth, and the liar sets himself at odds with it, whether on purpose or carelessly. Even being thrown around by pleasure and pain ends up unjust, he says, because it makes us unfair in how we treat people and things. Marcus's view rests on nature and the gods, and not everyone shares it. But his picture is easy to test on an ordinary day. The extra ten dollars, the excuse that wasn't true, the credit taken for someone else's work: on his view, none of them stays in its box, because the box was never separate. For Marcus we're one fabric, and a pulled thread puckers the whole cloth.

607.title: Death as a work of nature
607.hook: death is like teething, growing up, having children: one of nature's works (Meditations 9.3)
607.howItsDone: Stoic readers often reflect briefly on mortality as part of nature's ordinary course, alongside growing up and growing old, as a way of meeting it calmly rather than with dread.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pulled thread: one small wrong puckers the whole cloth. Your line was we're one fabric.

A baby is cutting teeth: fussy, drooling, awake at three in the morning. Nobody calls it a tragedy. It's hard, it hurts, and everyone in the house knows it's just what babies do on the way to growing up. Marcus picks up exactly that ordinary picture and sets it beside something we usually treat very differently. It's a tender subject, so gently: today we read his thought on dying.
screen: `A BABY CUTTING TEETH.` → `HARD, BUT NATURAL.` → `DEATH AS A WORK OF NATURE.`

segments.voice: In book nine Marcus writes: don't despise death, but be content with it, since it's one of the things nature wills. Then he names the others. Being young and growing old. Growing up and reaching full size. Getting teeth, a beard, gray hair. Conceiving, carrying a child, giving birth. All the works our seasons of life bring. Dying, he says, belongs on the same list. He doesn't say rush toward it, and he doesn't say ignore it. He says wait for it the way you'd wait for a child to be born: not anxious, not careless, knowing it comes in its own time. That, he says, is how a thoughtful person meets it. Then a homelier consolation, the kind that reaches the heart: think of the things you'll leave, and the habits of the people you'll no longer have to live among. But in the same breath he checks himself. Don't be offended with them, he writes. Care for them, and bear with them gently. This is a Stoic view, and not everyone holds it. Many traditions speak of death in terms of a soul, a judgment, a world to come, or rebirth, and Marcus himself, across the book, is unsure what follows. What he offers here isn't a teaching about the afterlife. It's a posture: to see dying as part of the same nature that brought teeth and gray hair, and so not to meet it with horror.

608.title: The wrongdoer wrongs himself
608.hook: whoever does wrong, wrongs himself first (Meditations 9.4)
608.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this line to turn anger toward someone who wronged them into something closer to pity, while still acting to protect themselves and others.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was cutting teeth: Marcus sets dying among nature's ordinary works. Your line was nature's work.

Someone cuts you off in traffic, then makes a rude gesture for good measure. In the moment there's only one victim, and it's you. But follow that driver home. The rest of their evening is still inside that anger. Their shoulders are still up; their day is still a little worse for it. Marcus wrote a very short entry in book nine about exactly this, two lines long.
screen: `CUT OFF IN TRAFFIC.` → `FOLLOW THEM HOME.` → `THE WRONGDOER WRONGS HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: In George Long's 1862 translation: “He who does wrong does wrong against himself.” Then Marcus adds: whoever acts unjustly acts unjustly toward himself, because he makes himself bad. For Marcus, the only real harm is harm to your character, the ruling part of you. Your car, your schedule, even your body can be damaged by someone else. Your goodness can be damaged only by you. So the person who wrongs you has, at most, dented your fender. They've dented their own self. If that's true, the wrongdoer isn't someone to hate. They're someone to pity, the way you'd pity a person who stepped on their own foot and then blamed the floor. That isn't looking down on them. It's seeing the injury clearly. The very next entry keeps this honest: a person can act unjustly by not doing something, too. So pity is no reason to stand by; standing by can be a wrong of its own. What shifts is the feeling underneath. Not, how dare they, but what did that cost them? And by Marcus's logic it cuts close to home: every time we snap, cheat, or lie, the first person changed is the one who did it.

609.title: Enough for now
609.hook: a present judgment, a present act, a present acceptance: that's enough (Meditations 9.6)
609.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations use this entry as a short evening check: did I see truly, act for others, and accept what came today? If so, the day was enough.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was George Long, whose translation says the wrongdoer wrongs himself. Your line was he's hurt himself.

Your phone shows you a hundred things you could want. A better kitchen, a different job, a calmer family, the trip, the body, the version of you that's on top of everything. The list never ends because it isn't built to end. Then, in book nine, Marcus writes an entry only one sentence long, and in George Long's English it finishes on a word that list never says. Enough.
screen: `A HUNDRED THINGS TO WANT.` → `A LIST BUILT NOT TO END.` → `ENOUGH FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: Marcus writes, roughly: your present judgment, grasping things as they are; your present action, done for the common good; your present acceptance of whatever comes from outside you. These are enough. Look at the parts. A judgment: seeing this moment truly. An action: doing this moment's work for others. An acceptance: being at peace with what this moment brought. Each one happens now. None of them needs a future that hasn't arrived. That's why enough is radical. So much of what drives us says not yet: not until the promotion, the cure, the apology. Marcus says the three things a good life needs are all available in the present, and that's sufficient. Not perfect. Sufficient. The Greek verb behind that word means it suffices. And the week, looking back: the spring runs clear, poured out, teach or bear, we're one fabric, nature's work, he's hurt himself, and now, it suffices. Seven entries, and every one pulls the same way: away from what other people do and what tomorrow might bring, toward what you can see, do and accept right here. Across books eight and nine, the lesson keeps coming back to the same small size: this moment, and three things you can do in it.

segments.voice: Name one thing about this exact moment you've been fighting, the noise, the tiredness, the weather, and without pretending to like it, say inside: this is what's here. Then check the three: am I seeing this moment truly, is there something good I can do in it, can I accept what it brought? If you can answer, that's enough.
Three presents. Marcus's list: a true judgment, an action for the common good, an acceptance of what comes. They suffice. Today's word.
Your line: it suffices. Judgment, action, acceptance: not perfect, just sufficient. That's the week, done.
